# **MCP Apps**

## **Background**

### **Prerequisites**

* Since MCP apps run in a webview, you'll need some experience writing client-side JavaScript.  
* Familiarity with basic JavaScript build processes will help, though that is not essential for this tutorial.  
* You don’t need to know TypeScript, just JavaScript\!

### **Why MCP apps?**

We’ve seen that MCP servers can add great value to an AI client experience. So much can be accomplished in the realm of text.

But sometimes passing text back and forth is insufficient. How about an application that needs images, a chart, or some audio? What if you need something genuinely interactive \- a form to fill out, a sortable table, or even a way to buy a plane ticket?

Enter MCP apps\!

### **What are MCP apps?**

MCP apps are a new extension to the MCP standard. They let your server do more than take text in and return text. They let you pop up a little web page, right there in the chat, where you can build your own interactive experience. They run in a sandboxed iframe, letting you implement whatever you could normally do in an iframe, including executing JavaScript, styling with CSS, playing audio files, and much more.

### **Where can I use them?**

[Many major AI clients](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/extensions/client-matrix) support MCP apps now, including ChatGPT, VS Code, Claude Desktop, claude.ai, Postman, and Cursor.

### **How do they work?**

You already know how to build tools. MCP apps let you attach a *webview* to a tool. When the tool loads, so does the webview. In FastMCP, that looks like this:

```python
@mcp.tool(app = {"resourceUri": “ui://my_webview”})
```

That webview contains your HTML, JavaScript, CSS, and so on. When the LLM asks to use your tool, the tool executes, and the host renders the associated resource in an \<iframe\> .

Once your webview starts, your JavaScript uses the `app.connect()` method to let the host know it’s ready. It associates the `app.ontoolresult` event with the code you’ll use to handle tool data. The host then passes your tool’s output into your iframe. This triggers that `toolresult` event, which your JavaScript responds to.

Your JavaScript can also use `app.callServerTool()` to call any tool in the server.

All of these `app` events and methods are implemented through the main way in which an iframe and its host page communicate:  `postMessage()`. 

## **Let’s build an MCP app**

### **What we’ll build**

Let’s start with something quite simple: an MCP app that pops up dog pictures. All the webview needs to do is display an image.

We’ll build:

* an MCP tool that calls a dogs API and returns the URL of an image  
* a view that requests this URL from the MCP tool, then pops that URL into an \<img\> tag

As always, we’ll usually show the smallest and simplest code that makes this work. The [samples in the ext-apps repo](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps) and the documentation provide more options.

### **Using a skill**

You can just use [the skill in the create-mcp-app skills area of the mcp repo](https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/blob/main/plugins/mcp-apps/skills/create-mcp-app/SKILL.md). Copy it to your MCP directory.

If your system has `wget`, you can use that:

```bash
wget https://raw.githubusercontent.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/refs/heads/main/plugins/mcp-apps/skills/create-web-app/SKILL.md
```

If not, there’s always `curl`:

```bash
curl -LO https://raw.githubusercontent.com/modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps/refs/heads/main/plugins/mcp-apps/skills/create-web-app/SKILL.md
```

(Use `-O` to keep the original filename, or `-o filename.md` to save it under a different name.)

If you want to learn to create an MCP app yourself, read on\!

### **The tool, Python version**

#### **Setup**

We used these in the last project:

```python
import requests
from fastmcp import FastMCP
```

For MCP apps, we add a new one:

```python
from fastmcp.apps import AppConfig, ResourceCSP
```

We need `AppConfig` to give our iframe the power to connect to external URLs. We’ll need this power twice:

* to call the API that returns URLs of dog pictures  
* to let the browser retrieve that image from an external domain

#### **Define some constants**

First, we define some constants relating to our resource. The `RESOURCE_URI` needs to start with the `ui://` protocol, but the rest can be any identifier you choose.

`viewResource` is a simple dictionary we just define here because we’ll use it for every tool that uses our webview.

```python
API_BASE_URL = "https://dog.ceo/api"
HTML_FILENAME = "view.html"
RESOURCE_URI = "ui://dog_image"

viewResource = {"resourceUri": RESOURCE_URI}
```

#### **Start up our server**

As always, FastMCP makes this simple.

```python
mcp = FastMCP("dogs")
```

#### **Our tool**

This is where things get interesting. As in past examples, our tool calls an API, massages the response, and returns a string. The key difference is that we pass the `@mcp` decorator a new argument: `app = viewResource` . This associates the tool with our webview resource.

```python
@mcp.tool(app = viewResource)
def get_random_dog() -> str:
    """Retrieves the URL of an image of a random dog."""
    response = requests.get(API_BASE_URL + "/breeds/image/random")
    json = response.json()
    return json["message"]
```

### **The view**

#### **Over”view”**

Notice that `view.html` includes CSS and JavaScript with the HTML. Normally we’d keep those in separate files and import them with `<style>` and `<script>` tags. 

But remember that our code is inside an iframe\! If our code tried to import an external CSS or JS file, like

```html
<script src="https://mydomain.com/dogs.js"></script>
```

This would work if the iframe was allowed to access mydomain.com. But it’s not easy to tell what domain an AI client will use for local development. Thus we keep these inline.

The best practice would be to introduce a simple build process to combine JS and CSS with HTML into a single file, letting us store these separately, and if you use TypeScript, of course, to transpile that to JS.

The CSS provided isn’t unique to this project, so let’s skip it for now.

### **The HTML**

Most of our HTML is standard boilerplate. Here’s the part that will appear to the user:

```html
<body>
  <img />
  <h2>It's a dog!</h2>
</body>
```

We have an image tag, and a little caption beneath it.

### **The JavaScript**

#### **import the MCP app library**

```js
import { App } from "https://unpkg.com/@modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps@0.4.0/app-with-deps";
```

This imports the MCP Apps client library for webviews \- the `App` class we’ll need to send and receive data from our tool, through the host, inside our iframe. If we’d written the server in TypeScript/JavaScript and had already installed the npm package as a dependency, we could have imported this from that local package:

```js
import { App } from "@modelcontextprotocol/ext-apps";
```

#### **Start up the app**

Now we can instantiate an `App` object for use here:

```js
const app = new App({ name: "Dog viewer", version: "1.0" });
```

The name is arbitrary.

#### **Handle tool results when they arrive**

When our tool returns data, the app receives a `toolresult` event. The event carries a `content` field \- an array of content blocks holding your tool's output. Each block has a `type` field that tells you what's inside:

* **`"text"`** — has a `text` string field  
* **`"image"`** — has `data` (base64 string) and `mimeType`  
* **`"audio"`** — has `data` (base64) and `mimeType`  
* **`"resource_link"`** — a reference to an MCP resource, with `uri`, `name`, and optional `title`, `mimeType`, `size`  
* **`"resource"`** — an embedded resource, either text or blob

Here, we expect a single `text` object. To keep this code very small, we assume we got one. In real life, you would want to check this. In particular, if the tool threw an error, you’d want to handle that situation, and the `text` object would not exist. Anyway, assuming that the tool has sent us the URL of an image, we inject that into the image’s `src` attribute to retrieve and display it.

```js
    app.ontoolresult = ({ content }) => {
      const imgUrl = content[0].text;
      const img = document.querySelector('img');
      img.src = imgUrl;
    };
```

#### **Connect to the host**

Finally, the app needs to connect to the host to signal that the webview is ready.

```js
await app.connect();
```

### **It works\!**

![][image1]

## **One more tool**

Now let’s add a slightly more elaborate tool. The Dogs API can fetch (get it?) pictures of a specific dog breed. We can build a tool around that which expects a string, passes that along to the API, and returns a dog picture. The API returns an array of every dog picture it has for that breed. We’ll just return the first one. For simplicity, we’ll once again skip the error-checking we’d very much desire in production.

```python
@mcp.tool(app = viewResource)
def get_dog_by_breed(breed: str) -> str:
    """Retrieves the URL of an image of a dog of a desired breed"""
    response = requests.get(f"{API_BASE_URL}/breed/{breed}/images")
    json = response.json()
    return json["message"][0]
```

Here’s the result:

![][image2]

Since Claude is smart and helpful, not only does it comment on the dog picture, but it will even try to fix your spelling. Here, I typed “dachsund”, and it immediately corrected that to “dachshund” before calling the tool.

But how do we know what dog breeds the API knows about? In particular, some dog breeds go by multiple names \- for example, pit bulls are also Staffordshire Terriers.

Of course, we could put that information into the tool… but why not use our new UI instead?

## **Adding interactivity**

Let’s add an HTML form to our view to let users pick their desired breed.

```html
<body>
  <img />
  <form>
    <select>
      <option value="">(choose one)</option>
      <option value="bullterrier/staffordshire">pit bull</option>
      <option value="doberman">doberman</option>
      <option value="malamute">malamute</option>
      <option value="pekinese">pekinese</option>
      <option value="pug">pug</option>
    </select>
    <button type="submit">Get my dog</button>
  </form>
</body>
```

Check `view_dropdown.html` for the full JavaScript. The key change is that we attach an event listener to this form’s `submit` event. When the user submits the form, we use `app.callServerTool()` to invoke the MCP server’s `get_dog_by_breed` tool, receive the string the tool generates, and drop that into the `<img>` tag's `src` attribute.

```js
    form.addEventListener("submit", async (e) => {
      e.preventDefault();
      const breed = select.value;
      if (!breed) return;

      const result = await app.callServerTool({
        name: "get_dog_by_breed",
        arguments: { breed },
      });
      
      updateImgUrl(result?.content);
    });
```

If you make these changes, close Claude, and restart it, you’ll find all your dog server webviews have been replaced by the new one.

![][image3]

## **Debugging**

When we wrote tools, we relied on a few resources for debugging:

* The [MCP Inspector](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/docs/tools/inspector)  
* Claude’s logfiles

The logfiles are still an invaluable way to see what Claude is doing with tools. But, once again, the MCP Inspector makes things easier. Conveniently FastMCP provides [an inspector for MCP apps](https://gofastmcp.com/apps/development). Start it up with

```bash
fastmcp dev apps
```

It starts your MCP server, lets you run a tool with an associated webview, and then pulls up a webpage with your webview working. If things don’t look right, you can visit your browser’s developer tools to debug.

In fact, since Claude Desktop operates in a Chromium browser, it kindly lets you use Chrome DevTools to inspect the Desktop UI. You can open it using the standard Ctrl-Option-I (Command-Option-I on Macs) shortcut. In this case, to look right at what’s happening in your view, you can right-click on the view and choose “Inspect Element”. This opens DevTools and brings you right to your HTML.

![][image4]

## **Error-checking**

To keep the code compact, we omitted basic error checking. Of course, not only would be essential to add this for production code, but these checks would help you debug during development as well.

First of all, not all hosts support MCP apps. You can check each client’s context to find out. You’ll need to add these imports:

```python
from fastmcp import Context
```

```python
from fastmcp.apps import UI_EXTENSION_ID
```

And then each tool should check as follows:

```python
@mcp.tool(app=AppConfig(resource_uri="ui://my-app/view.html"))
async def my_tool(ctx: Context) -> str:
    if ctx.client_supports_extension(UI_EXTENSION_ID):
        # Return data optimized for UI rendering
        return rich_response()
    else:
        # Fall back to plain text
        return plain_text_response()
```

There’s more:

* In the server, ensure the Dogs API returns something, and if it does that it returns what you expected  
* In the view, ensure that the DOM elements you depend on exist, and make sure that the MCP server tools return what you expected
